items.passage:
The Crow and the Jug

It was the hottest day of the summer. A crow had flown a long way and she was very thirsty.

At last she saw a tall jug standing by a garden wall. There was a little water at the very bottom. The crow pushed her beak into the jug, but it was too narrow and the water was too low. She could not reach it.

She tried to tip the jug over, but it was too heavy.

The crow did not give up. She looked around and saw some small pebbles on the path. She had an idea.

She picked up one pebble and dropped it into the jug. Plop! Then another, and another. Each pebble pushed the water up a little higher.

After fifty pebbles, the water was right at the top. The crow drank and drank until she was not thirsty any more.

Little by little does the trick.

items.passage:
The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse

A country mouse lived in a field. One day her cousin from the town came to visit. The country mouse gave him barley, beans and a drink from the stream.

“How can you eat such plain food?” said the town mouse. “Come to the town with me. I will show you how to live!”

So they went to the town. In a big house, on a long table, there were cakes, cheese and jelly left over from a party. The country mouse could not believe her eyes.

But just as she took her first bite, the door burst open. A cook came in with a broom! Then a cat sprang out from under a chair. The two mice ran for their lives and hid in a tiny hole, shaking.

When it was quiet again, the country mouse picked up her bag.

“Thank you, cousin,” she said. “But I would rather eat beans in peace than cake in fear.”

And she went home to her quiet field.

items.passage:
The Dog and His Reflection

A dog was trotting home with a big juicy bone in his mouth. He felt very pleased with himself.

On the way he had to cross a little bridge over a stream. As he crossed, he looked down into the water.

There he saw another dog, with another big bone! The dog did not know he was looking at his own reflection.

“That bone looks even bigger than mine,” he thought. “I want it too.”

So he opened his mouth to grab the other bone and gave a loud bark. Splash! His own bone fell into the stream and sank to the bottom.

The other dog had vanished, and so had the bone. The dog walked home sadly with nothing at all.

If you are greedy, you can lose what you already have.

items.passage:
The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs

A farmer and his wife had a very special goose. Every morning she laid an egg made of shining gold.

The farmer sold the eggs at the market, and soon he and his wife were rich. They bought new clothes, a new cart and a fine horse.

But the farmer was not happy. “One golden egg a day is too slow,” he grumbled. “The goose must be full of gold inside. If we open her up, we can have all the gold at once!”

His wife agreed. So they did. But inside, the goose was just like any other goose. There was no gold at all.

And now there would never be any more golden eggs.

The farmer and his wife sat down and cried. They had been too impatient, and they had lost everything.

Wanting too much, too quickly, can leave you with nothing.

items.passage:
The Oak and the Reed

A tall oak tree stood beside a river. Down by the water grew a thin green reed.

“Look at you,” said the oak. “You bend over whenever a little breeze blows. I am strong. I never bend for anyone.”

The reed said nothing.

That night a great storm came. The wind howled and roared. The reed bent low, right down to the water, and let the wind rush over it.

The oak stood straight and proud. It would not bend. The wind pushed and pushed. Then, with a terrible crack, the oak broke and crashed into the river.

In the morning the sun came out. The little reed stood up again, as green as ever.

It is sometimes wiser to bend than to break.

items.passage:
The Rain Race

The Grand Prix had just begun when the rain came. Big drops drummed on the track and the road turned shiny and slippery.

Blaze was in the lead. Turbo was right behind him, trying hard to catch up.

On the sharpest corner, Turbo’s wheels lost their grip. He spun round and round and slid off the track into the gravel. His wheels whirred, but he was stuck.

Blaze saw him in his mirror. He could keep going and win the race easily. But he remembered how Turbo had once been kind to him.

Blaze slowed down, turned off the track and drove up behind Turbo. “Hold on!” he called. He pushed with his front bumper. Turbo’s wheels found the grass, then the road.

The other cars zoomed past them both. Turbo and Blaze crossed the line together, last of all, covered in mud.

The crowd cheered louder for them than for the winner.

“We came last,” said Turbo.

“No,” said Blaze, smiling. “We came together.”

The Grand Prix had just begun when the rain came. Big drops drummed on the track and the road turned shiny and slippery.

Blaze was in the lead. Turbo was right behind him, trying hard to catch up.

On the sharpest corner, Turbo’s wheels lost their grip. He spun round and round and slid off the track into the gravel. His wheels whirred, but he was stuck.

Blaze saw him in his mirror. He could keep going and win the race easily. But he remembered how Turbo had once been kind to him.

Blaze slowed down, turned off the track and drove up behind Turbo. “Hold on!” he called. He pushed with his front bumper. Turbo’s wheels found the grass, then the road.

The other cars zoomed past them both. Turbo and Blaze crossed the line together, last of all, covered in mud.

The crowd cheered louder for them than for the winner.

“We came last,” said Turbo.

“No,” said Blaze, smiling. “We came together.”

Bleep and the Broken Satellite

High above the Earth, a weather satellite had stopped working. Without it, nobody could tell whether a storm was coming.

Captain Nova flew her spaceship up close to the satellite. She floated out in her spacesuit, with Bleep the droid tucked under her arm.

There was a small hatch on the side of the satellite. Captain Nova opened it and peered in. “The broken part is right at the back,” she said. “My hands are much too big to reach it.”

Bleep beeped bravely. He was small. He could fit.

Slowly, carefully, Bleep squeezed through the hatch. Inside it was dark and full of wires. He switched on his headlight. There it was: a loose bolt, wobbling in its hole.

Bleep reached out his little tool arm and turned the bolt, tighter and tighter, until it would not wobble any more.

The satellite’s lights blinked on. Blue, green, blue.

Back on Earth, the weather maps came to life again.

“Being small,” said Captain Nova, “is exactly what we needed today.”

items.passage:
The Desert Rally

Rosa’s team were racing across the desert. The sand was golden and the sky was bright blue.

Then, far away, a brown cloud rose up. It grew bigger and bigger. “Sandstorm!” shouted Rosa.

The wind whipped up the sand until nobody could see more than a few steps. The racing car spluttered and stopped. Sand had blocked its air filter, and the engine could not breathe.

Rosa pulled on her goggles and tied a scarf over her nose and mouth. She tied a rope from the truck to her belt, so she could not get lost.

Then she walked out into the storm, step by step, holding the rope.

She found the car, opened the bonnet and took out the filter. It was full of sand. She tapped it, shook it and blew on it until it was clean, then clicked it back in place.

The engine coughed, then roared.

When the storm passed, the team cheered. They did not win the rally, but every single car in their team reached the finish.

One morning {hero} woke up with a terrible cold. Achoo! When the hero tried to fly, nothing happened. When the hero tried to lift the sofa, it would not budge. The superpowers had gone, just for the day.

That afternoon a little girl ran up, crying. “My kitten is stuck on the roof of the library!”

{hero} looked up at the high roof. With no flying, how could anyone get up there?

The hero thought hard. Then the hero ran to the fire station and knocked on the door. “I need your tallest ladder,” said {hero}, “and some help to hold it.”

The firefighters carried the ladder over and held it tight. {hero} climbed up, step by step, legs shaking a little. It was a long way down.

At the top, the kitten was hiding behind a chimney. {hero} spoke softly until the kitten crept close, then tucked it inside a warm jacket and climbed down again.

The little girl hugged her kitten.

items.passage:
The Knight and the Dragon

Every night a loud, sad roar echoed around Castle Rook. The people were frightened. “There is a dragon in the hills,” they said. “It will eat us all!”

Sir Rowan, the youngest knight, put on his armour and rode into the hills. He was scared, but he kept going.

In a dark cave he found the dragon. It was enormous and green, with smoke curling from its nose. Sir Rowan held up his shield.

But the dragon did not attack. It just sat there, holding out one huge foot and groaning.

Sir Rowan looked closer. A long, sharp thorn was stuck in the dragon’s toe!

Very carefully, the knight took hold of the thorn and pulled. Out it came. The dragon sighed a long, warm sigh of relief.

The next morning, Sir Rowan rode back to the castle with the dragon flying above him. The people screamed, until they saw the dragon land gently and bow its head.

From that day on, the dragon lived at Castle Rook. Every winter it lit all the fires in the great hall with one puff, and nobody was cold again.

Maya and Sam were having a sleepover at the dinosaur museum. Their sleeping bags were laid out right under the giant skeleton of a Diplodocus.

When the lights went out, the museum was very quiet and very dark.

Then they heard it. A low rumbling, growling noise. GRRRRRR.

“A dinosaur!” whispered Sam, pulling his sleeping bag over his head.

Maya was scared too, but she wanted to find out. She switched on her torch and followed the sound, past the T. rex teeth and the fossil eggs, round the corner and into the next hall.

There stood Mr Patel the cleaner, pushing a big floor-polishing machine. GRRRRRR, it went, as it spun round and round.

Mr Patel laughed. “Did I wake you? Come and see something special.”

He shone his torch on a glass case. Inside was a real fossil footprint, as big as Maya’s sleeping bag.

“That was made by a dinosaur that walked here millions of years ago,” said Mr Patel.

Maya ran to fetch Sam. Being brave, she decided, was much more fun than hiding.

items.passage:
Little Benjamin did not very much want to see his Aunt.

He came round the back of the fir-tree, and nearly tumbled upon the top of his Cousin Peter.

Peter was sitting by himself. He looked poorly, and was dressed in a red cotton pocket-handkerchief.

“Peter,” said little Benjamin, in a whisper, “who has got your clothes?”

Peter replied, “The scarecrow in Mr. McGregor’s garden,” and described how he had been chased about the garden, and had dropped his shoes and coat.

Little Benjamin sat down beside his cousin and assured him that Mr. McGregor had gone out in a gig, and Mrs. McGregor also; and certainly for the day, because she was wearing her best bonnet.

Peter said he hoped that it would rain.

At this point old Mrs. Rabbit’s voice was heard inside the rabbit hole, calling: “Cotton-tail! Cotton-tail! fetch some more camomile!”

Peter said he thought he might feel better if he went for a walk.

They went away hand in hand, and got upon the flat top of the wall at the bottom of the wood. From here they looked down into Mr. McGregor’s garden. Peter’s coat and shoes were plainly to be seen upon the scarecrow, topped with an old tam-o’-shanter of Mr. McGregor’s.

Little Benjamin said: “It spoils people’s clothes to squeeze under a gate; the proper way to get in is to climb down a pear-tree.”

Peter fell down head first; but it was of no consequence, as the bed below was newly raked and quite soft.

It had been sown with lettuces.
items.passageSource: Beatrix Potter, The Tale of Benjamin Bunny (1904)

items.passage:
Jemima Puddle-duck became quite desperate. She determined to make a nest right away from the farm.

She set off on a fine spring afternoon along the cart-road that leads over the hill.

She was wearing a shawl and a poke bonnet.

When she reached the top of the hill, she saw a wood in the distance.

She thought that it looked a safe quiet spot.

Jemima Puddle-duck was not much in the habit of flying. She ran downhill a few yards flapping her shawl, and then she jumped off into the air.

She flew beautifully when she had got a good start.

She skimmed along over the tree-tops until she saw an open place in the middle of the wood, where the trees and brushwood had been cleared.

Jemima alighted rather heavily, and began to waddle about in search of a convenient dry nesting-place. She rather fancied a tree-stump amongst some tall fox-gloves.

But—seated upon the stump, she was startled to find an elegantly dressed gentleman reading a newspaper.

He had black prick ears and sandy coloured whiskers.

“Quack?” said Jemima Puddle-duck, with her head and her bonnet on one side—“Quack?”

The gentleman raised his eyes above his newspaper and looked curiously at Jemima—

“Madam, have you lost your way?” said he. He had a long bushy tail which he was sitting upon, as the stump was somewhat damp.

Jemima thought him mighty civil and handsome. She explained that she had not lost her way, but that she was trying to find a convenient dry nesting-place.

“Ah! is that so? indeed!” said the gentleman with sandy whiskers, looking curiously at Jemima. He folded up the newspaper, and put it in his coat-tail pocket.
items.passageSource: Beatrix Potter, The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck (1908)

items.passage:
When the three kittens were ready, Mrs. Tabitha unwisely turned them out into the garden, to be out of the way while she made hot buttered toast.

“Now keep your frocks clean, children! You must walk on your hind legs. Keep away from the dirty ash-pit, and from Sally Henny Penny, and from the pig-stye and the Puddle-Ducks.”

Moppet and Mittens walked down the garden path unsteadily. Presently they trod upon their pinafores and fell on their noses.

When they stood up there were several green smears!

“Let us climb up the rockery, and sit on the garden wall,” said Moppet.

They turned their pinafores back to front, and went up with a skip and a jump; Moppet’s white tucker fell down into the road.

Tom Kitten was quite unable to jump when walking upon his hind legs in trousers. He came up the rockery by degrees, breaking the ferns, and shedding buttons right and left.

He was all in pieces when he reached the top of the wall.

Moppet and Mittens tried to pull him together; his hat fell off, and the rest of his buttons burst.

While they were in difficulties, there was a pit pat paddle pat! and the three Puddle-Ducks came along the hard high road, marching one behind the other and doing the goose step—pit pat paddle pat! pit pat waddle pat!

They stopped and stood in a row, and stared up at the kittens. They had very small eyes and looked surprised.

When the three kittens were ready, Mrs. Tabitha unwisely turned them out into the garden, to be out of the way while she made hot buttered toast.

“Now keep your frocks clean, children! You must walk on your hind legs. Keep away from the dirty ash-pit, and from Sally Henny Penny, and from the pig-stye and the Puddle-Ducks.”

Moppet and Mittens walked down the garden path unsteadily. Presently they trod upon their pinafores and fell on their noses.

When they stood up there were several green smears!

“Let us climb up the rockery, and sit on the garden wall,” said Moppet.

They turned their pinafores back to front, and went up with a skip and a jump; Moppet’s white tucker fell down into the road.

Tom Kitten was quite unable to jump when walking upon his hind legs in trousers. He came up the rockery by degrees, breaking the ferns, and shedding buttons right and left.

He was all in pieces when he reached the top of the wall.

Moppet and Mittens tried to pull him together; his hat fell off, and the rest of his buttons burst.

While they were in difficulties, there was a pit pat paddle pat! and the three Puddle-Ducks came along the hard high road, marching one behind the other and doing the goose step—pit pat paddle pat! pit pat waddle pat!

They stopped and stood in a row, and stared up at the kittens. They had very small eyes and looked surprised.
items.passageSource: Beatrix Potter, The Tale of Tom Kitten (1907)
